claims.text: The equimolar HfNbTaTiZr alloy is a BCC solid solution.
The equilibrated, defect-minimized equimolar alloy has a lattice constant of 3.403 Å.
Changing Nb or Ta concentration while compensating with Hf changes atomic-scale lattice distortion and solid-solution homogeneity.
Reducing Nb or Ta from 20 at.% to 10 at.% produces limited lattice distortion and a more homogeneous solid solution.
The more homogeneous 10 at.% Nb or Ta alloy pins dislocations more effectively and reduces dislocation mobility.
The 10 at.% Nb or Ta variants have greater ultimate tensile strength and elastic modulus than the equimolar alloy.
The 10 at.% Nb or Ta variants have a lower effective thermal-expansion mismatch and consequently lower mismatch-induced thermal stress than the equimolar alloy.
Increasing Nb or Ta from 20 at.% to 30 at.% creates substantial atomic-size and crystal-structure mismatch and local heterogeneity.
The local heterogeneity in the 30 at.% Nb or Ta variants lowers resistance to dislocation motion.
The 30 at.% Nb or Ta variants have lower strength and elastic modulus than the equimolar alloy.
The 30 at.% Nb or Ta variants have a higher effective thermal-expansion coefficient or mismatch and therefore develop larger thermal stresses.
Mechanical and thermoelastic responses vary nonmonotonically with Nb or Ta concentration.
Increasing temperature weakens the favorable effect of the more homogeneous solid solution because lattice vibrations become stronger.
At 300 K, the equimolar alloy has an ultimate tensile strength of approximately 2.9 GPa, an elastic modulus of approximately 117.7 GPa, and an elongation of 17.0%.
The equimolar alloy has a linear thermal-expansion coefficient of 1.96 × 10^-5 K^-1.
A modified embedded-atom-method potential used for the proposed simulations is validated for this alloy and the relevant responses.
Nb or Ta contents of 10, 20, and 30 at.% can be compared under otherwise matched MD conditions, with Hf providing the compositional balance.
Failure of the 10 at.% variants to increase strength and reduce thermal-expansion mismatch, or failure of the 30 at.% variants to decrease strength and increase mismatch, would reject the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention states that both tensile and thermal-expansion tests are performed over 300–1200 K, whereas the conditions and falsification design place the tensile comparison primarily or exclusively at 300 K and only sweep temperature for thermal expansion.

The intervention and falsification design specify 10–30 at.% or discrete 10/20/30 at.% variants, while the stated applicability boundary extends the variation to 0 at.% without specifying or testing that endpoint.
